result.summary: Pausanias begins his tour of Greece at Attica's coast: Sunium, Laurium, and the harbours of Phalerum, Piraeus and Munychia. He recounts the history of the harbours, Themistocles' tomb and the sights and temples near them.

scenes.title: Sunium and Laurium coast
scenes.summary: The promontory of Sunium, its temple of Athene, Laurium's silver mines and Patroclus' island are described. The island's name leads to a note on the Ptolemaic fleet sent against Athens.

scenes.title: Harbours of Athens and Themistocles
scenes.summary: Phalerum was the old port; Themistocles made the Piraeus the port. His tomb is there, and his sons returned from exile.

scenes.title: Sights of the Piraeus
scenes.summary: The gold statues of Athene and Zeus, a painting of Leosthenes, the portico and Conon's temple of Aphrodite are described, with a note on Aphrodite at Cnidus.

scenes.title: Munychia, Phalerum and Colias
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists shrines at Munychia and Phalerum, the altar of Androgeos, the promontory of Colias and the burnt temple of Hera on the road to Athens.

alias_notes.explanation: The Cnidians' name for the temple others call Athene of Cnidus.

analysis.text: The opening sets the book's method: a traveller's tour that mixes monuments with local history and tradition.
Pausanias writes in the Roman period and treats Athens' wars, Persian, Macedonian and Egyptian, as fading history recorded in monuments.

fun_facts.text: The temple of Athene at Sunium survives as ruins, and the cape remains a famous landmark.

language_notes.text: A palisade is a fence of stakes; Patroclus fortified the island as a naval base during this campaign.
"Township" means a small settlement or deme, not a harbour town.
"Exhumed" means dug up. Themistocles died in exile in Magnesia in Asia Minor, so his bones were brought back secretly.
Leosthenes led the Greeks in the Lamian War (323–322 BC) against Macedonian rule after Alexander's death; he was killed besieging Lamia.
Conon's victory off Cnidus in 394 BC destroyed Spartan sea power; Lacedæmonians means Spartans.
"Tutelary saint" is the translator's phrase for a guardian deity. Doritis, Acræa and Fair Voyage are cult titles of the goddess.
Jason sailed to Colchis on the Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece; Phalerus is said to have been among the Argonauts.
The Persian fleet was wrecked after the battle of Salamis (480 BC); a stade is about 200 metres.
Mardonius was the Persian general who occupied and burnt Athens in 479 BC.

context_notes.text: The silver mines at Laurium financed Athens' fleet; the temple at Sunium was a landmark for sailors.
Themistocles, the Athenian statesman who built up the fleet before Salamis, developed the Piraeus as Athens' main harbour around 493 BC.
Demos means the Athenian People, personified as a deity. Leochares was a famous fourth-century BC sculptor.
Androgeos, son of Minos, was killed in Attica, which led to Athens paying tribute to Crete.

literary_notes.text: Athens regrets mistreating the man it exiled, and honours his bones only after his death.
Pausanias flatters himself and knowledgeable readers as scholars, showing his pride in antiquarian learning and his authorial voice.
The closing remark suggests the surviving statue escaped the burning, a wry, skeptical aside on local tradition.
